title: What makes an act good (CCC 1750–1756)
hook: the act itself, the intention and the circumstances

segments.voice: Yesterday, called to beatitude: the moral life begins with the happiness a person is made for. Your line was made for happiness.

Sunday, the collection basket comes down the pew. Three envelopes go in. The first is from a woman who heard the parish is helping a family that lost its home in a fire. The second is from a man who folds his so the person beside him can see how thick it is. The third is from a woman who lost her job last month and gave anyway, less than she used to. From the back of the church, all three look identical. What makes an act good?
screen: `THREE ENVELOPES, ONE BASKET.` → `SAME ACT FROM THE BACK PEW.` → `WHAT MAKES IT GOOD?`

segments.voice: The Catechism answers with three things, which it calls the sources of morality. First, the object: what is actually chosen. Giving money, telling the truth, telling a lie. Reason looks here first, and some acts are wrong whatever the reason behind them. Second, the intention: why, the end a person has in view. One intention can run through a whole string of actions, and one action can carry several intentions. Third, the circumstances: who, where, when, how much, under what pressure. Then how they fit, and the Catechism is plain. A good intention can't make a bad act good. Its example is lying: even to help a neighbor, a lie is still a lie. In one short phrase: the end does not justify the means. It goes the other way too: a bad intention can spoil a good act. The example comes from Jesus, about giving alms to be seen. In the Douay-Rheims: "sound not a trumpet before thee." The man folding his envelope for the pew is doing a good thing for a hollow reason. Circumstances can make an act more or less good, more or less serious; fear, for instance, can lessen a person's responsibility. But they can't turn a wrong act into a right one. So a good act needs all three together: a good object, a good intention, fitting circumstances. And the third envelope? Thinner, maybe. But a lost job and a tight month add weight to that gift.

segments.voice: Bring up one decision in front of you this week: a message to send, money to spend, a favor to say yes or no to. Name the what plainly, then the why, honestly, even if it's a little embarrassing, then the when and how: who's affected, the timing, the pressure. Notice which of the three is the shaky one, and if you pray, ask for light on that one.
What makes an act good. The Catechism names three sources: the act chosen, the intention, and the circumstances, and asks that all three be good together. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT MAKES AN ACT GOOD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what, why, when. The week ran from covenant and the domestic church, through sacramentals, popular piety and funerals, to beatitude and today. Week done; rest well.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching weighs an act by its object, its intention and its circumstances, and some Catholics use those three in an examination of conscience before confession.

options: The Catechism says a good intention can't make a bad act good: the end does not justify the means.
Yes. The Catechism says only your intention counts, so the act itself doesn't matter at all.
Yes. The Catechism says circumstances decide everything, so pressure can make any act right.
chat.meaning: The Catechism names three sources of morality: the act, the intention and the circumstances. A good intention can't make a bad act good.

notes: CCC 1750–1756 paraphrased (copyrighted translation): three sources (1750), object (1751), intention (1752), good intention doesn't justify lying, 'the end does not justify the means', almsgiving for vainglory (1753), circumstances (1754), all three together (1755), some acts wrong regardless (1756). Confirm.
Hook's three envelopes are an invented illustration; the third (a gift after a lost job) shows a circumstance increasing an act's goodness (CCC 1754). A Keeper may prefer a different example.
